title: How the Web Works
summary: A browser finds a server, requests a page, and turns the response into something you can use.

subtopics.title: Website name lookup
subtopics.explanation: DNS finds a network address for a website name. People remember names more easily than numeric addresses. It is like looking up a business in an address book. DNS lookup can take time, and cached answers may be reused for a while. For example, a typed domain name must resolve before a browser can connect to its server. For example, use the Network panel to see which request is waiting before the page appears.

subtopics.title: Secure connection
subtopics.explanation: HTTPS protects information traveling between the browser and server. TLS helps establish an encrypted connection and check the server identity. It is like sealing a letter and checking the address before delivery. HTTPS protects the connection, but it does not prove the website’s content is trustworthy. For example, a secure connection is established before private form data travels to the website. For example, check whether a cached DNS answer removes a lookup on repeat visits.

subtopics.title: Request and response
subtopics.explanation: HTTP is the message format browsers and servers use. The browser asks for a resource; the server replies with a status and content. It is like placing an order and receiving a receipt with the result. Methods and status codes help describe what the request means and what happened. For example, a GET request can ask a server for a product page and receive a status code. For example, a certificate warning means the browser could not establish expected identity.

subtopics.title: Page files
subtopics.explanation: The first response often points to other files, such as stylesheets, scripts, and images. The browser requests those files to complete the page. It is like receiving assembly instructions that refer to more parts. A page can look incomplete while required resources are still loading. For example, an HTML response may trigger more requests for CSS, scripts, and images. For example, distinguish a server status from a browser connection failure when reporting an error.

subtopics.title: Rendering
subtopics.explanation: The browser interprets HTML and CSS, runs JavaScript, and draws the page. This process turns instructions into pixels and interaction. It is like assembling a model from a plan. Large files or expensive scripts can delay what a person sees, so measure loading and rendering. For example, a slow script can delay interaction even after the browser has displayed some content. For example, reducing unnecessary round trips can help users on distant or mobile networks.

foundations.overview: When someone opens a website, the browser finds its server, creates a connection, requests files, and turns the response into a page. DNS helps find the server address; HTTPS protects traffic; HTTP carries requests and responses. Think of it like looking up a business, calling it securely, and asking for a document. The browser then loads extra files and renders what people see.
foundations.whyItMatters: A page depends on several network and browser stages. Tracing them in order helps diagnose delays and explains what HTTPS does—and does not—protect.
commonUseCases: Trace why a page takes time before its first response.
Explain the browser’s requests for a page and its assets.
Separate connection security from application authorization.

commonMisconceptions.myth: HTTPS proves that a website is honest.
commonMisconceptions.reality: HTTPS protects the connection and identifies a domain; it does not guarantee trustworthy content.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser downloads only one file for a web page.
commonMisconceptions.reality: HTML can reference stylesheets, scripts, fonts, and images that require further requests.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A fast connection guarantees a fast page.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Server response, file size, JavaScript work, and rendering also affect user-perceived speed.

keyTakeaways: DNS finds a network address for a website name.
HTTPS protects information traveling between the browser and server.
HTTP is the message format browsers and servers use.
The first response often points to other files, such as stylesheets, scripts, and images.
The browser interprets HTML and CSS, runs JavaScript, and draws the page.
